blocks.content: Meghalaya's path to statehood is distinctive for having passed through an intermediate 'autonomous state within Assam' stage before achieving full statehood — a two-step formation process worth knowing precisely, since it's a frequently tested sequence.

Following Independence, the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills were initially incorporated as autonomous districts within the state of Assam, governed under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution (Chapter 5) — a framework specifically designed to grant a degree of tribal self-governance over local matters while these hill areas remained formally part of the larger state.

Growing regional demands for greater self-governance and, eventually, full separation from Assam — driven by concerns over inadequate representation and cultural/political distinctiveness from the Assamese-majority plains — led to a two-stage formation process for Meghalaya, distinct from a single, one-step creation.

cells: The Assam Reorganisation (Meghalaya) Act, 1969 passed by Parliament, providing for the creation of an 'autonomous state' within Assam

Meghalaya comes into existence as an AUTONOMOUS STATE within Assam (an intermediate constitutional category, with its own Governor-appointed administration and legislative arrangements, but not yet a full separate state)

The North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 passed by Parliament, providing for full statehood for Meghalaya (along with Manipur and Tripura, covered in the companion Manipur GS volume) and creating Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram as new Union Territories
Meghalaya attains FULL STATEHOOD, formally separating from Assam, on the same date as Manipur and Tripura

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Meghalaya's TWO-STAGE formation — first as an 'autonomous state' WITHIN Assam (2 April 1970), then as a FULLY separate state (21 January 1972) — is a distinctive and frequently tested sequence, differentiating Meghalaya's formation process from most other Indian states' single-step creation.

Williamson A. Sangma became Meghalaya's first Chief Minister upon the attainment of full statehood in January 1972 (having earlier also led the state during its 1970-72 autonomous-state period), and is regarded as one of the principal architects and founding figures of the modern Meghalaya state, alongside his broader role in articulating the case for Khasi-Jaintia-Garo self-governance distinct from wider Assam.

items: Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills initially incorporated as Sixth Schedule autonomous districts within Assam post-Independence.
Meghalaya became an AUTONOMOUS STATE within Assam on 2 April 1970 (Assam Reorganisation (Meghalaya) Act, 1969).
Meghalaya attained FULL STATEHOOD on 21 January 1972 (North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971), together with Manipur and Tripura.
Williamson A. Sangma = Meghalaya's first Chief Minister (from 1972; also led the 1970-72 autonomous-state administration).
